Satire. A literary mode that uses wit, irony, ridicule, and dark humor to critique and expose human vice, folly, corruption, or social injustice. Employing indirect methods of mockery and exaggeration rather than direct moral argument, satire ranges from gentle mockery to savage denunciation and has been a powerful tool of social commentary from classical antiquity to the present day.

Satire originated in classical Rome. Horace practiced a mild, conversational satire while Juvenal delivered bitter, scathing indictment. These two established poles of the form that persist in all later satire. The central technique is irony—saying the opposite of what is meant, or appearing to endorse vice to expose its absurdity. This indirection allows satire to evade censorship and engage readers intellectually.

Satire uses exaggeration and grotesque distortion to render the absurdity of vices visible. Through hyperbole, social conventions reveal themselves as arbitrary or repugnant. Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal, published in seventeen twenty-nine, proposed the eating of Irish children as a solution to poverty. It became the paradigm of mordant satirical logic, using deadpan reason to condemn inhumanity.

The targets of satire vary. Personal satire mocks individual folly or vice, as Alexander Pope's Dunciad does. Social satire exposes class hypocrisy, pretense, and corruption, as Voltaire's Candide does. Political satire attacks rulers and systems, as George Orwell's Animal Farm does. Satire is distinct from comedy, which aims chiefly to amuse, and from parody, which imitates a specific work. Satire aims at moral correction and social reform through ridicule.

Satire is often dangerous to its author. Censorship, libel suits, and political persecution have accompanied satire throughout history, from Juvenal to Salman Rushdie. Yet its power lies precisely in this danger—the satirist speaks truths that power wishes suppressed.

Swift remains the master of ironic satire. His A Modest Proposal remains the gold standard of savage critique. Pope's The Rape of the Lock and Dunciad satirize literary and social pretense with formal brilliance. Voltaire uses mock-optimism to demolish philosophical complacency. Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Connecticut Yankee critique racism and imperialism through vernacular humor. George Orwell's twentieth-century political satire used animal fable and dystopia to expose totalitarianism. And the classical tradition continues through these later examples—Juvenal's bitter, invective style established the model of satirical denunciation, while Horace's urbane, conversational tone models a gentler, more personal satire.
